welcome: Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm. In Volume 01, Imaan and Akhlaq began learning what Islam teaches and how acts of worship guide everyday life. This second volume is for learners aged nine to ten. It develops deeper understanding without expecting children to resolve complicated juristic disputes or speak about private health and family matters in public.

journeys.title: My Muslim Identity
journeys.aim: Faith becomes stronger as we understand its meaning and let it guide our choices.

lessons.title: Faith Is More Than a Label
story: The class was organising a small “Guidance and Good Choices” exhibition. Akhlaq offered to make a poster with his name in enormous golden letters. “That way,” he said, “everyone will know I am a good Muslim.”

Imaan did not laugh. She asked him to think about what the poster was actually saying. “Does large writing show what is in our hearts?” Akhlaq shook his head. Their teacher, Sir Zameer, placed three cards on the table: BELIEVE, SPEAK, ACT. He asked the children to put them in an order that made sense.

Mohsina said that a person first learns what is true. Mohsin suggested that words should tell the truth. Imaan said actions ought to agree with our words. The teacher explained that Islamic books discuss the detailed meaning of Imaan carefully, but all learners should understand that merely boasting about faith does not make a person honest.

At lunchtime Akhlaq discovered that someone had left a notebook behind. He returned it quietly instead of asking for applause. The owner thanked him. Akhlaq decided to make the poster smaller and change its title to: “What I Believe Should Help Me Do Good.”
Dadi Jaan later reminded him that Allah knows the hearts. Our work is to learn, obey, repent and treat people justly—not to place spiritual scores on classmates.

teaching.text: Islam begins with faith in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. The master chapter explains belief in the heart and its expression, and shows that knowledge should guide conduct. A person should not confuse being praised by others with sincerity before Allah. Good character does not replace Salah or the other obligations of Islam; rather, worship and character must be learned together. If we make mistakes, repentance and repairing harm matter more than pretending to be perfect. Only Allah knows hearts. Children must not decide which classmates are “real believers” from outward performance.

questions.q: Is being Muslim only a name or family label?
questions.a: No. It involves genuine belief and seeking to follow Allah’s guidance.

questions.q: Can we judge another person’s sincerity?
questions.a: No. Allah knows what is in hearts.

questions.q: Does honesty replace Salah?
questions.a: No. Islam teaches both worship and good character.

questions.q: What should we do after harming somebody?
questions.a: Acknowledge the wrong, seek forgiveness and try to put it right.

reflect: When do I care more about being noticed than about doing the right thing?

scenario: A classmate forgets their book. You can return it privately or announce your generosity to the whole school. What is the better response, and why?
decide.feedback: Returning it quietly protects the classmate’s dignity and avoids showing off. A sincere good action need not become a performance.

lessons.objective: Explain how faith, speech and actions belong together without judging other people’s hearts.

lessons.title: The Shahādah and the Choices We Make
story: For the school exhibition, the children were making audio cards. Visitors could press a button to hear a phrase and its meaning. Akhlaq proposed recording the Shahādah very fast. “If I can say it without a pause, I must know it perfectly,” he said.

Salamah listened to his practice at home. “You remember the sounds,” she replied, “but can you explain what they mean?” Imaan offered to be the visitor and ask questions. Akhlaq said that Allah alone deserves worship and that Muḥammad ﷺ is His servant and Messenger. He paused at the second statement. “Why do we say servant as well as Messenger?”

Salaam explained that Muslims love and follow the Prophet ﷺ but worship Allah alone. The Prophet brought the guidance of Allah; following him includes learning his worship and his honesty, mercy and justice.
At school a pupil asked whether learning the declaration meant that Akhlaq had never made a mistake. “No,” he replied, smiling. “It means that I know the guidance I am trying to follow.”
The children recorded the words slowly with their teacher. On the card they added a second button: “Explain the meaning.” It was the button Akhlaq now liked best.

teaching.text: The Shahādah testifies that only Allah is worthy of worship and Muḥammad ﷺ is His servant and Messenger. These two truths belong together: Tawḥīd directs worship to Allah alone; Risālah means we accept the Messenger’s authentic guidance. Learning Arabic pronunciation matters, but memorising sounds without understanding should not be the final goal. This lesson revisits the foundation introduced in Volume 1 and asks for greater understanding. Expressions of faith must never be used as a game for judging someone else’s inner belief.

questions.q: What does the first testimony affirm?
questions.a: That Allah alone deserves worship.

questions.q: What does the second testimony affirm?
questions.a: That Muḥammad ﷺ is Allah’s servant and Messenger.

questions.q: Why does understanding matter?
questions.a: Our words should express belief and guide our choices.

questions.q: Does the Shahādah mean a person is already perfect?
questions.a: No. Every learner must continue learning and correcting mistakes.

reflect: What part of the testimony guides the way I treat others?

scenario: Your friend knows the Arabic words but struggles to explain their meaning. Do you laugh, make them repeat faster or help patiently?
decide.feedback: Help patiently. Correct learning combines accurate words, understanding and gentle teaching.

journeys.title: Knowing Allah and the Unseen
journeys.aim: Creation invites thoughtful questions; revelation teaches what we cannot discover by senses alone.

lessons.title: The World Invites Us to Think
story: Akhlaq found an unfamiliar seed in the school garden. He drew it in his notebook, then tried to guess what it would become. Mohsin said it would be a flower. Mohsina thought it might be a vegetable. Nobody was certain, so they asked their science teacher how they could find out.

The teacher suggested observing its leaves over time, recording sunlight and water, and comparing it with a reliable guide. “Good questions lead us to examine evidence,” she said. “They do not require us to invent answers.”

That evening Akhlaq showed his drawing to Sheikh Uncle. “If science can explain how plants grow, why do we need to think about Allah?” he asked. Sheikh Uncle said that learning how something grows is a valuable study of the created world. The question of why creation exists and depends on Allah is different from the question of how a plant uses light and water.

Imaan added a heading to the garden record: “Observe carefully, be grateful, ask wisely.” She explained that their religious understanding came from the Qur’an, while the plant identification would come from observation and study.
A week later the seedling finally showed its first recognisable leaves. Akhlaq was delighted; he had learned the plant’s name and gained a deeper reason to appreciate the world around him.

teaching.text: The Qur’an invites people to reflect upon the heavens and the earth. The master chapter introduces dependence and the question of a Creator; older learners will explore its philosophical vocabulary in greater depth. At ages 9–10 we begin by distinguishing two good questions: scientific study asks about patterns and processes in creation, while Islamic belief affirms that the created world depends upon Allah. Do not claim every scientific discovery proves a specific religious interpretation. Our duty is to observe honestly, use reliable explanations and ask thoughtful questions without pretending to know what has not been established.

questions.q: Does Islam discourage careful study of nature?
questions.a: No. Reflecting on creation and learning from it are encouraged.

questions.q: What does an experiment help investigate?
questions.a: How something behaves or happens under observed conditions.

questions.q: Who does Islam teach is the Creator?
questions.a: Allah, who depends on nothing He created.

questions.q: What should we do when an observation surprises us?
questions.a: Check it carefully rather than inventing an answer.

reflect: Do I ask questions to learn, or only to appear clever?

scenario: Your partner announces a plant’s identity without checking. Is it better to repeat the guess confidently or verify it?
decide.feedback: Check the evidence. Honest inquiry is a good habit in both religious learning and ordinary study.

lessons.objective: Recognise that observing creation can awaken thoughtful questions about our Creator.
lessons.dailyAction: Observe one natural process for several days and write what you actually notice, not what you only expect.

lessons.title: The Six Articles of Faith Together
story: Sir Zameer prepared six envelopes for the library project. Each envelope carried a question: What do Muslims believe about Allah? Who are the angels? Why are books revealed? Who brings Allah’s message? What happens after this life? What does Qadar teach us?

Akhlaq wanted to open the last envelope first. “Qadar sounds difficult,” he admitted. Imaan said they could learn the basic meaning today and study its harder questions later. The children placed the envelopes around a central page labelled ĪMĀN.

At home, Dadi Jaan explained that belief in angels and the Hereafter is not based on meeting them in a science classroom. We learn of them through Allah’s revelation and authentic teachings. “Can I draw an angel from my imagination?” Akhlaq asked. Dadi reminded him that pictures of unseen realities should not be presented as factual descriptions when the sources have not told us their appearance.
Mohsina suggested that every envelope also include one responsible action. Belief in the Hereafter could encourage honesty. Belief in revelation could encourage listening to Qur’an with respect.
The children were careful: an action was not itself the definition of an article of faith. But understanding their beliefs could make their ordinary choices more thoughtful.

teaching.text: The Ḥadīth of Jibrīl names belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day and divine decree. The master manuscript treats these across several chapters, including detailed explanations reserved for later ages. At this level children should state each article accurately and recognise the difference between what the senses can observe and what authentic revelation teaches. A general belief in Qadar does not remove a person’s responsibility for choices; its more difficult questions belong to the advanced level.

questions.q: How many principal articles of faith are taught in the Ḥadīth of Jibrīl?
questions.a: Six.

questions.q: Name two articles concerning the unseen.
questions.a: For example, angels and the Last Day.

questions.q: What is the source of knowledge about angels?
questions.a: Allah’s revelation and authentic Prophetic teaching.

questions.q: Does Qadar excuse deliberate wrongdoing?
questions.a: No. We remain responsible for our decisions.

reflect: Which belief helps me remember that my choices matter?

scenario: A friend thinks an imagined drawing proves how angels appear. How could you explain the difference between illustration and revelation?
decide.feedback: Explain kindly that we must not present an invented depiction as a fact about the unseen.

lessons.objective: Name the principal articles of faith and know that some realities are learned through revelation.
lessons.dailyAction: Memorise the six articles with understanding, and choose one good action that reflects responsibility.
lessons.tryTogether: Make six respectful concept cards using words and symbols such as a book or a clock; do not depict Allah, angels or Prophets.
lessons.keyWords: Īmān — faith; Ghayb — unseen; Qadar — divine decree.
lessons.parentNote: Keep discussion age-appropriate and hopeful; avoid frightening depictions of the Hereafter or speculative descriptions of angels.

lessons.title: Questions About Allah: Thinking With Humility
story: A classmate asked Akhlaq, “If everything needs a maker, who made Allah?” Akhlaq felt embarrassed because he could not answer at once. He went home convinced he had failed a test.

Salaam listened carefully. “A thoughtful question does not mean you have failed,” he said. “But first we need to distinguish created things from the One whom Islam teaches is not created.” He reminded Akhlaq of Sūrah al-Ikhlāṣ and explained that Allah is not an object inside the universe waiting for somebody else to make Him.

Imaan took out two kinds of cards: things that begin and depend on other things, and the Islamic description of Allah as eternal and independent. “We should not put Allah into the created-things pile,” she said.

When Akhlaq returned to school he explained that his faith did not claim everything, including Allah, was created. He also admitted that he had more questions and wanted to learn carefully as he grew older.

Sir Zameer praised that last sentence. Knowledge was not a race in which a child had to answer every philosophical question before lunchtime. The class added a question box to their exhibition: “Questions worth studying with a reliable teacher.”

teaching.text: Created things begin, change and depend on causes and conditions. In Islamic belief, Allah is the Creator, eternal and independent; He is not a created object requiring another creator. The master discussion uses deeper terms such as “necessary” and “contingent,” but our aim here is to introduce the distinction without presenting complex philosophical arguments as settled by one classroom analogy. Honest questions should be welcomed and answered with reliable knowledge, not ridicule.

questions.q: Does Islamic belief describe Allah as created?
questions.a: No. Allah is eternal and unlike His creation.

questions.q: What Sūrah teaches that none is comparable to Allah?
questions.a: Sūrah al-Ikhlāṣ.

questions.q: Must a child know every difficult answer immediately?
questions.a: No. Learning can take time and good teachers.

questions.q: Is asking a sincere question disrespectful?
questions.a: No. Ask respectfully and seek reliable answers.

reflect: When do I feel afraid to admit that I do not know something?

scenario: Someone laughs at another child’s question about Allah. What is the responsible response?
decide.feedback: Protect the right to ask respectfully, and seek a trusted knowledgeable explanation.

journeys.title: Revelation and the Messenger
journeys.aim: We understand Prophethood and honour the Companions while checking religious claims carefully.

lessons.title: Why Allah Sent Messengers
story: Akhlaq was practising giving directions to a new pupil. He drew a map from the gate to the library but forgot to mark the staircase. The pupil followed his instructions and arrived at the wrong classroom.

“Directions must be complete,” Imaan said. Sheikh Uncle overheard them and asked a larger question: if people need guidance for small journeys, how do they learn to worship Allah correctly? Dadi Jaan explained that Allah sent Messengers who taught His guidance. The Qur’an records that Messengers called people to worship Allah and turn away from false worship.

Mohsin asked whether the Prophets were ordinary teachers who invented religious rules. “No,” Sheikh Uncle replied. “They were human beings chosen by Allah and entrusted with revelation. We do not imagine the details of their lives, or call our school examples events from their history.”
The children reviewed what they already knew about Muḥammad ﷺ: he is Allah’s servant and final Messenger, and Muslims learn his Sunnah with love and care.
Later they corrected the missing staircase on the school map. Imaan wrote: “A complete map helps a person find a classroom. Revelation guides us in matters beyond any school map.”

teaching.text: Prophets and Messengers convey guidance from Allah. The master chapter discusses revelation, trustworthy character, signs of Prophethood and why Muslims follow Muḥammad ﷺ. He is the final Prophet. At this age, the main goals are to distinguish revelation from personal opinion, know the Prophet ﷺ as human and honoured, and understand that love for him includes learning his worship and character. The full examination of proofs and difficult objections remains an older learner’s task.

questions.q: Who sends Messengers?
questions.a: Allah.

questions.q: What is one central message of the Messengers?
questions.a: Worship Allah alone.

questions.q: Who is the final Prophet?
questions.a: Muḥammad ﷺ.

questions.q: Why do Muslims study the Sunnah?
questions.a: To learn and follow the Messenger’s authentic guidance.

reflect: How can I show love for the Prophet ﷺ in the way I speak and act?

scenario: A pupil says the Prophet ﷺ should be worshipped because Muslims love him deeply. How would you correct this?
decide.feedback: Teach respectfully that we love and obey the Messenger ﷺ but worship Allah alone.

lessons.objective: Explain that Allah sent Messengers to guide people and that Muḥammad ﷺ is the final Messenger.
lessons.dailyAction: Choose one authentic Prophetic teaching about manners and practise it at home.
lessons.tryTogether: Make a two-column page labelled “Allah alone is worshipped” and “the Messenger ﷺ teaches guidance.”
lessons.keyWords: Nubuwwah — Prophethood; Waḥy — revelation; Sunnah — Prophetic guidance.
lessons.parentNote: No portrayal of the Prophet ﷺ; use Qur’an, books and neutral visual motifs. Verify every narrated teaching.

lessons.title: Companions: Learning Faithful Service
story: For their exhibition, the children chose a wall of “People Who Helped Good Knowledge Reach Others.” Akhlaq wanted to place only famous names on it. Mohsina asked whether ordinary helpers had mattered too.

Dadi Jaan explained that the Ṣaḥābah were those who met the Prophet ﷺ as believers and died upon Islam, with technical detail studied by scholars. They learned directly from him and transmitted his teaching. The Muhājirūn left their homes for Allah’s sake, and the Anṣār gave support in Madinah.
Mohsin chose to make the poster about the four Rightly Guided Caliphs. Imaan added a note that the Companions included many women as well as men who learned, taught and served.

“Does honouring them mean we should quarrel about which child knows the most names?” Akhlaq asked. Salamah shook her head. “Respect should encourage us to learn accurately and speak with good manners.”

On the exhibition day the class assigned roles fairly: one child checked names, another read the references, and another helped visitors. Their display no longer celebrated fame alone. It celebrated trustworthiness, learning and service.

teaching.text: The Qur’an praises early believers and mentions the Muhājirūn and Anṣār. The master chapter also introduces the four Rightly Guided Caliphs and the meaning of Allah’s righteous servants. Our focus at ages 9–10 is accurate recognition and respect, not controversial debates about historical disputes. We honour the Companions while remembering that Prophethood is unique and not earned by ordinary people.

questions.q: Who were the Ṣaḥābah?
questions.a: Believing companions of the Prophet ﷺ, according to the recognised scholarly definition.

questions.q: Who were the Muhājirūn?
questions.a: Believers who emigrated for their faith.

questions.q: Who were the Anṣār?
questions.a: Supporters who welcomed and helped in Madinah.

questions.q: What should admiration for the Companions encourage?
questions.a: Accurate learning, humility and service.

reflect: Do I value the quiet work of helpful people?

scenario: You notice a poster leaves out all women who helped preserve Islamic knowledge. How can you improve it?
decide.feedback: Add verified examples respectfully, recognising that beneficial knowledge has been preserved by women and men.

lessons.objective: Recognise who the Ṣaḥābah were and learn why service and truthful transmission matter.
lessons.dailyAction: Learn one verified example of a Companion’s service and perform a small useful task yourself.

lessons.title: Miracles, Righteous People and Checking Claims
story: One afternoon a video circulated among the children claiming that a strange light in a window proved somebody had become a great saint. Mohsin was impressed. Akhlaq wanted to share the video before school ended.
Sheikh Uncle asked what the class actually knew. The video did not tell them where the event happened or whether it had been edited. The children tried to identify the source but could not.

In their lesson, Sheikh Uncle explained that a Muʿjizah is an extraordinary sign given by Allah to a Prophet. Classical scholarship also discusses Karāmah in connection with righteous servants. But a video with mysterious music is not reliable evidence of religious rank. People should be respected for faith, truthful conduct and their service, not because they advertise wonders.
Imaan suggested making a checklist for the exhibition: Is the claim from the Qur’an or an authentic narration? Is the source identified? Are we inventing details? Could sharing it mislead somebody?
Akhlaq deleted the unsourced message from his draft. He realised that checking a spectacular claim was not a sign of weak faith. It was a way to protect the truth from careless rumours.

teaching.text: The master chapter distinguishes Muʿjizah (a miraculous sign associated with a Prophet) from Karāmah (an extraordinary favour in traditional discussion of righteous people). Neither turns a person into a Prophet, and neither should become an excuse to accept dishonest claims. The best evidence for what Allah revealed is reliable religious scholarship. Children should not attempt to reproduce miracles, make judgments about another person’s closeness to Allah or share sensational reports without checking.

questions.q: What is a Muʿjizah?
questions.a: A miraculous sign that Allah grants to a Prophet.

questions.q: Is a surprising internet video automatically proof of a miracle?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: What is a better standard for judging someone’s conduct?
questions.a: Truthfulness, worship and recognised good character.

questions.q: What should we do with a doubtful religious message?
questions.a: Pause, check its source and consult a knowledgeable adult.

reflect: Do I share surprising news before checking it?

scenario: An unknown account says sharing a dramatic clip earns a special religious reward. Do you forward it immediately?
decide.feedback: No. Rewards and religious claims require sound evidence; ask a trusted scholar or teacher.

lessons.objective: Distinguish Prophetic miracles from everyday tricks and avoid passing along unchecked religious claims.
lessons.dailyAction: Choose one online claim and practise asking who said it, where it came from and whether a trustworthy source confirms it.
lessons.tryTogether: Create a “Check before you share” bookmark for the school library.
lessons.keyWords: Muʿjizah — Prophetic miracle; Karāmah — extraordinary favour; Taḥqīq — verification.
lessons.parentNote: No supernatural gameplay or staged “miracles”; keep source hierarchy and child online-safety rules clear.

journeys.title: The Foundations of Islamic Rulings
journeys.aim: We begin to understand why the jurists use different names for obligations and recommended acts.

lessons.title: Fard, Wajib and Sunnah: Why Words Matter
story: Akhlaq took a small shopping list to the corner shop. Some items had to be bought for dinner; others were optional treats. When he came home, he announced that all items on a list must have the same importance. Imaan asked whether ice cream was really as necessary as drinking water.

Father used the example to introduce a more serious idea: the words used by Muslim jurists distinguish duties, recommendations and forbidden actions. “A shopping list is not a book of Fiqh,” he warned, “but it helps us notice why categories matter.”

The children opened the master chapter. They found Fard, Wajib, Sunnah, Mustaḥab, Mubāḥ, Makrūh and Ḥarām. Akhlaq was surprised to learn that Hanafi scholars distinguish Fard and Wajib in ways not identical to the terminology of every other Sunni school.
At the exhibition, a visitor asked whether a Sunnah was therefore unimportant. Akhlaq answered that something need not have the same legal consequence as a Fard to deserve love and care.

Sir Zameer helped them correct one card that had declared every disliked action equally prohibited. “Learn the exact category from a qualified source,” he said. “Do not build rulings from your own guesses.”

teaching.text: Fiqh is the scholarly understanding of religious rulings from evidence. In the Hanafi framework, Fard and Wajib are both duties but have a technical distinction. Sunnah names Prophetic guidance and has specialised legal usages; Mustaḥab or Mandūb describe encouraged actions; Mubāḥ is permitted; Ḥarām is forbidden; and Makrūh requires distinguishing types in Hanafi study. Other Sunni schools may use these terms differently. Children need the pattern, not independent authority to issue rulings.

questions.q: What does Fiqh study?
questions.a: Religious rulings and how they are understood from evidence.

questions.q: Are Fard and Wajib identical technical terms in Hanafi Fiqh?
questions.a: No. They are distinguished in the Hanafi method.

questions.q: Does Sunnah always mean optional and unimportant?
questions.a: No. Its uses are more detailed.

questions.q: Can a child invent a ruling by choosing a label?
questions.a: No. Rulings must be learned from reliable scholarship.

reflect: When I hear an unfamiliar religious word, do I ask what it means?

scenario: Your friend says every Sunnah is a Fard. Do you agree to avoid disagreement or ask a teacher?
decide.feedback: Ask respectfully. Legal classifications require correct definitions and evidence.

lessons.parentNote: Do not substitute game categories for a legal fatwa. Explain four-school differences only if the exact examples are verified.

lessons.title: Worship Needs Intention and Understanding
story: The school organised a cleanup day. Mohsin swept the floor because the teacher had assigned him. Akhlaq swept too—but then kept announcing that his corner was cleaner than everyone else’s.

At home Imaan asked Salaam whether a good action changed when someone did it only for praise. He explained that intentions matter, though nobody at school could claim to know another child’s heart. He also reminded them that intention alone does not replace learning how an act of worship is actually performed.

“Could we invent an extra movement in Salah if we meant well?” Akhlaq asked. “No,” replied Father. “The prescribed forms of worship are learned from the Messenger ﷺ. We can be creative with classroom posters, not with the essentials of rituals.”

The children returned to the exhibition plan and wrote two headings: “Do the right thing” and “Do it for the right reason.” Under the first they placed learning an accurate Wudu sequence. Under the second they placed gratitude and sincerity.

When cleanup day ended, Akhlaq discovered that Mohsin had quietly stacked the chairs without any instruction. This time he did not compete with him. They thanked one another and finished the job together.

teaching.text: The five pillars are acts of worship with prescribed foundations. Sincere intention helps us seek Allah’s pleasure, but the correct method must also be learned. An apparently kind everyday act does not replace obligatory worship. Conversely, outward performance without truthfulness and responsibility should prompt us to examine our own conduct. The master text connects all these elements while warning against judging others’ sincerity.

questions.q: Why do intentions matter?
questions.a: They concern why we act and whether we seek Allah’s pleasure.

questions.q: Can a good intention change the required form of Salah?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Does kindness remove the obligation to pray?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Can we reliably know another person’s inner intention?
questions.a: No. Allah knows hearts.

reflect: Would I still do a helpful task if nobody praised me?

scenario: You want to add an invented ritual step to make prayer “more special.” What should you do?
decide.feedback: Follow the correctly taught prayer rather than inventing a new ritual requirement.

lessons.objective: Understand that correct worship combines sincere intention with learning the prescribed method.
lessons.dailyAction: Carry out one helpful activity sincerely and learn one worship rule from a trusted teacher.

journeys.title: Purity and Care
journeys.aim: We practise the normal Hanafi purification methods and learn when special help is needed.

lessons.title: Clean Water, Ordinary Dirt and Ritual Purity
story: For the exhibition science table, Mohsina brought jars of clear water, cloudy water and garden soil. Akhlaq assumed the cleanest-looking jar must always be suitable for everything. Their teacher explained that water safety needs evidence, and a jar can look clear while still being unsafe to drink.

Later Salamah introduced the separate question of ritual purity. Ordinary mud on a sleeve is not automatically Najāsah. A person might have a visibly clean body and yet need Wudu because a ritual state has ended. A stain might also need identifying rather than being treated as dangerous simply because it looks dark.

Imaan asked why the old Fiqh books contained detailed rules about wells and quantities of water. Dadi Jaan said that the books addressed real historical circumstances. Qualified teachers study those principles carefully, while modern water hygiene also needs appropriate scientific assessment.
The class updated its display with two separate labels: “Is this water safe to drink?” and “What is its status for purification?” They were related concerns but not interchangeable questions.
Akhlaq wrote in his notebook, “Do not decide by a guess, and do not be afraid of every speck of dirt.”

teaching.text: Ṭahārah includes ordinary cleanliness and the legal state needed for worship. The master chapters distinguish actual impurity (Najāsah) from the state requiring Wudu or Ghusl. They also preserve classical Hanafi discussions of water and wells. At ages 9–10, focus on reliable ordinary practice: use suitable clean water, remove confirmed impurity, and avoid treating all dust or mud as Najis. Classical bucket counts are not a safe method for declaring modern drinking water fit for consumption.

questions.q: Is ordinary garden mud always Najāsah?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Can a person look clean but still need Wudu?
questions.a: Yes.

questions.q: Are drinkability and ritual suitability exactly the same question?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Who should answer complicated water questions?
questions.a: A qualified teacher or scholar, with water-safety professionals where needed.

reflect: Have I ever turned uncertainty about cleanliness into repeated checking?

scenario: You see a dry mark on a school uniform with no evidence it is impure. Should you declare the whole uniform unusable?
decide.feedback: No. Do not label things impure without grounds. Ask a trusted adult if a real concern exists.

lessons.title: Wudu: The Four Hanafi Obligatory Actions
story: Akhlaq had practised Wudu for years, but now Sheikh Uncle asked him an unfamiliar question. “Which parts are essential according to the Hanafi school, and which belong to the complete Sunnah method?”
Akhlaq started to say that everything must have exactly the same legal status. Imaan reminded him of the Fiqh categories they had just learned.

They stood beside a basin with a parent supervising. Sheikh Uncle named the four Hanafi Fard actions: washing the whole face, washing both arms including the elbows, wiping at least the required part of the head, and washing both feet including the ankles. He then guided them through the full taught sequence, including washing the hands first, rinsing mouth and nose properly, and the Sunnah manner of wiping.

The children slowed down at the arms. Mohsin had almost stopped below the elbows. They corrected the action without teasing him. Next they practised turning off the tap while rubbing water over a limb.

Akhlaq asked whether understanding the four Fard actions meant that the Sunnah steps could be discarded casually. “No,” Sheikh Uncle replied. “We learn the complete Prophetic way and distinguish its legal parts so we worship carefully, not carelessly.”

teaching.text: In Hanafi Fiqh the four obligatory actions of Wudu are washing the face; washing both arms including elbows; wiping at least the legally required portion of the head; and washing both feet including ankles. The full Sunnah method also includes other prescribed practices, among them beginning with Bismillāh and the sequence of rinsing and washing. The master chapter warns against missing elbows, ankles and areas that must be washed, and against wasting water or repeating checks from doubt. Details may differ in other schools. A qualified teacher must demonstrate the full method accurately.

questions.q: Must the elbows be included when washing the arms?
questions.a: Yes.

questions.q: Is the head washed or wiped in Wudu?
questions.a: Wiped in the prescribed manner.

questions.q: Must the ankles be included when washing the feet?

decide.feedback: Offer kind help and learn accurately. Correction should not become humiliation.

lessons.title: When Must Wudu Be Renewed?
story: One morning Akhlaq finished Wudu and sat down to tie his shoes. “What if I blinked too many times?” he asked Imaan. “Would I have to start again?” She laughed, then realised he was genuinely worried.

Salamah brought the relevant teaching notes. Some events really do end Wudu, while many ordinary actions do not. Using the toilet is different from closing your eyes briefly; sleep also has detailed rulings, depending on its condition. Children should learn common cases without treating every movement or passing feeling as proof that Wudu is lost.

At school, Sir Zameer gave each group a set of fictional cards. One described using the toilet. Another described picking up a pencil. A third described merely worrying that Wudu had ended, without evidence. The children sorted the cards with care and left complicated cases on a pile marked “Ask a teacher.”
Akhlaq noticed that the pile helped him. He did not have to guess an answer to every case before praying. After checking what he actually knew, he walked calmly to the prayer area.
That evening he wrote: “A real reason matters. Doubts do not deserve endless attention.”

teaching.text: Wudu must be renewed after recognised invalidators under the relevant fiqh rules. The original Hanafi chapter discusses different kinds of discharge, sleep and other cases. For this age, teach common clear examples and distinguish them from ordinary actions or unsupported fears. Repeating Wudu because of a passing doubt can create distress. Unusual medical situations or persistent uncertainty require suitable scholarly guidance; children must not receive definitive personal rulings from an app quiz.

questions.q: Does using the toilet normally require renewing Wudu before Salah?
questions.a: Yes.

questions.q: Does picking up a book break Wudu?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Should an uncertain feeling always lead to repeating Wudu?
questions.a: No. Follow reliable guidance and do not act on mere doubt.

questions.q: What about difficult or recurring personal cases?
questions.a: Ask a qualified adult or scholar rather than guessing.

lessons.title: Ghusl: Learning with Dignity and Privacy
story: Imaan noticed a new section in the learning binder marked “Private Questions.” She asked Salamah why a book for children included a lesson that could make some classmates feel shy.

Salamah explained that growing children deserve accurate knowledge before they need it, and that body-related questions should not become jokes or public tests. She told Imaan that Ghusl is not merely an ordinary shower when Islamic law requires a ritual bath.

For the classroom lesson Sir Zameer taught the general rules without asking any child about their personal circumstances. He explained the three Hanafi Fard actions: rinsing the mouth, rinsing the nose appropriately, and washing the entire body so the required areas are reached. The full Sunnah method would be demonstrated through a modest teacher guide, never through acting out private bathing in front of other pupils.
Akhlaq asked whether someone could seek help if illness made washing harmful. “Yes,” said Sir Zameer. “Islamic law has rules for genuine hardship; the exact answer depends on the situation.”

At home the children could each write a private question for a caregiver. Nobody was asked to read it to the class. Imaan appreciated the rule: knowledge could be taught openly while personal details remained confidential.

teaching.text: Ghusl is the prescribed ritual bath required in specified circumstances. The Hanafi essentials are rinsing the mouth, rinsing the nose, and washing the whole body without leaving an obligatory area unwashed. There is also a fuller Sunnah method. The master chapter discusses occasions when Ghusl is obligatory, recommended or subject to genuine exemptions. Learners approaching puberty need accurate, private explanations of menstruation and other maturity-related issues before these become relevant to them. Teachers must not assume every child develops at the same age.

questions.q: Is every ordinary shower automatically a complete Ghusl?
questions.a: Not necessarily; the prescribed conditions must be fulfilled.

questions.q: Name the three Hanafi obligatory Ghusl actions.
questions.a: Rinse the mouth, rinse the nose and wash the whole body as required.

questions.q: Should private bodily questions be discussed publicly?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: What if water could cause medical harm?
questions.a: Seek professional health and qualified fiqh advice.

decide.feedback: Maintain respectful privacy and help the learner reach a trustworthy adult.

lessons.title: Masah: When Islam Allows a Concession
story: It was a cold morning when Mohsin arrived at the academy wearing sturdy winter footwear. He had heard that travellers could sometimes wipe over suitable footwear rather than wash their feet in each Wudu. He wondered whether this meant any socks at any time.

Sheikh Uncle said the rule had conditions. In Hanafi Fiqh, qualifying khuffs or footwear must meet specified requirements, and they must be put on after complete purification. The permitted wiping period is ordinarily a day and night for a resident and three days and nights for a traveller, counted according to the legal rule. Special details depend on circumstances.

Imaan noticed that their classmate had a bandaged hand from a minor injury. She asked whether wiping a wound dressing was the same as wiping khuffs. “They are different legal discussions,” said Sheikh Uncle. “Never remove a medically needed dressing just to pass a classroom test.”
The group made two instructional cards: “qualifying footwear” and “medical dressing.” On both they added the same sentence: “Learn conditions from a qualified source.”
Akhlaq suggested a third card: “Mercy is not carelessness.” The teacher approved. They had discovered how a concession could make worship easier without turning every shortcut into a religious rule.

teaching.text: Masḥ over qualifying footwear is an established concession with conditions described in the master Hanafi chapter. It is not permission to wipe over every ordinary sock, nor to ignore the requirements for complete Wudu before wearing the footwear. The main periods are normally twenty-four hours for a resident and seventy-two for a traveller, with legal details governing their start and interruption. Wiping over a splint or medical dressing follows a different set of rules. Personal injury cases require medical and qualified fiqh advice.

questions.q: Does every sock automatically qualify for Masah?
questions.a: No. The footwear must satisfy the relevant rules.

questions.q: What should happen before qualifying footwear is put on?
questions.a: A complete valid Wudu, as required by the rules.

questions.q: Are the ordinary wiping periods identical for residents and travellers?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Is a medical dressing the same legal case as khuffs?
questions.a: No.

scenario: You see a friend with a bandage and want to remove it to demonstrate Wudu. Is that appropriate?
decide.feedback: No. Protect health and dignity; ask a qualified adult for the correct concession.

lessons.title: Tayammum: Purification During Genuine Difficulty
story: During a family trip, the car stopped at a rest area. A sign said that a water supply had been temporarily interrupted. Akhlaq worried that nobody would be able to pray.

Salaam explained that Allah has permitted Tayammum when its proper conditions are met. But they should first investigate whether usable water was genuinely available nearby and whether there was sufficient time and a safe way to obtain it. A broken tap at one sink did not automatically prove that water was unavailable everywhere.

Later Sheikh Uncle demonstrated the approved Hanafi classroom method on a suitable clean earth-related surface: make the intention and follow the taught wiping of the face and arms. He explained that the original chapter lists three Hanafi essentials and specifies how the method is performed. It is a legal alternative in defined circumstances, not a pretend game to replace Wudu whenever someone feels lazy.

Imaan asked about a person whose doctor had advised them not to wet a serious wound. Sheikh Uncle said medical evidence and a qualified scholar’s guidance mattered; children should not improvise treatment.

The family found safe suitable water before prayer time ended that day, so they made ordinary Wudu. Akhlaq was satisfied. Learning Tayammum had made him more grateful for a concession, not more eager to use it without reason.

teaching.text: The Qur’an permits Tayammum in specified circumstances involving water unavailability or relevant harm. The master Hanafi chapter teaches intention, wiping the face, and wiping the arms including elbows, with an established method. Technical questions about material, timing, recovery and illness require careful instruction. Children should not replace available safe water with Tayammum for convenience. At the same time, a genuine difficulty is not a reason for shame: the permission itself is part of Allah’s guidance.

questions.a: When prescribed conditions such as unavailable or harmful water are met.

questions.q: Does a broken tap at one sink always mean water is unavailable?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: What parts are wiped in the taught Hanafi method?
questions.a: The face and arms as prescribed.

questions.q: Who helps with illness-related rulings?
questions.a: A qualified scholar and appropriate health professional.

reflect: Do I appreciate permissions in the religion without misusing them?

scenario: A child wants to skip ordinary Wudu even though safe water is readily available. What should you explain?

journeys.aim: We learn prayer conditions, essential actions and good habits in congregation.

lessons.title: Seven Things to Check Before Salah
story: Akhlaq had been practising Salah at home. On the day of the class prayer demonstration he unfolded his mat, faced a wall and announced that he was ready. Imaan had another question. “How do you know the prayer time has begun?” He had forgotten to check.

Sir Zameer made a gentle correction. The master book lists seven conditions before Salah: a ritually clean body, clean clothing, a clean place, proper covering, the correct time, facing Qiblah, and intention. Some are physical preparations; some require knowing the prayer and direction.

Mohsin picked up a dusty mat. “Does any dust cancel the prayer?” he asked. The teacher reminded him that ordinary dust is not automatically a legal impurity. Mohsina suggested a timetable card to avoid guessing prayer times.

Together they checked the prayer place, covering and timetable. Then Imaan asked whether she had to say the intention in Arabic aloud. “Intention is in the heart,” said Sir Zameer. “Know which prayer you are performing for Allah.”

The next time Akhlaq prepared for Salah he checked his conditions once calmly. His preparation had become more accurate, but also less anxious. That was the goal: learn the requirements, use reliable information and begin worship without unnecessary fear.

teaching.text: The master chapter preserves seven prerequisites for Salah: Tahir body, clothing and place; covering the Satr; correct prayer time; facing Qiblah; and Niyyah. They are conditions before prayer, not the internal Fard acts performed during it. Some legal details depend on the kind of impurity, medical situations or differing juristic methods of calculating prayer times. Children should learn one reliable ordinary method and avoid repeated checking without cause. A simple clean place and suitable clothing are sufficient; expensive accessories are not required.

questions.q: How many conditions are listed before Salah in the original text?
questions.a: Seven.

questions.q: Is facing Qiblah one of them?
questions.a: Yes.

questions.q: Must a specific Arabic intention be spoken aloud?
questions.a: No. Intention is in the heart.

questions.q: Are these seven conditions the same as the internal prayer pillars?
questions.a: No.

reflect: Does being organised help me worship with more calm attention?

scenario: You are ready to pray but have not checked whether the time began. What should you do?
decide.feedback: Check a reliable timetable, then begin when the correct prayer time has entered.

lessons.title: Inside Salah: Fard, Wajib and Calm Worship
story: Akhlaq was delighted that he had memorised the movements of a Rakʿah. But at the school demonstration he rushed from bowing to prostration so fast that Mohsin could hardly follow.
Sheikh Uncle asked him to slow down. “Prayer is not a race to complete movements,” he said. “We must learn what is essential and perform it with attention.”

They opened Chapter 32 of the master text. It taught six Fard requirements in its Hanafi presentation: the opening Takbīr, standing where required, Qur’anic recitation, bowing, two prostrations and the final sitting for its required duration. The teacher then explained that Hanafi books distinguish additional Wajib acts and Sunnah forms.

Imaan wondered why people sometimes held their hands in different ways. Sheikh Uncle explained that recognised juristic schools discuss some prayer details differently. The children were to learn their taught Hanafi method correctly while respecting other Muslims following valid scholarly instruction.

For the exhibition the group filmed only a teacher-approved diagram of the prayer sequence, not a child racing against a timer. Akhlaq asked to add a reminder: “Take enough time to worship with calmness.”
The class agreed. Correctness mattered, but so did humility and the desire to worship Allah sincerely.

teaching.text: Salah contains indispensable actions, Wajib duties and Sunnah guidance, described in detail in the source chapter. The master Hanafi presentation lists six Fard elements, including the opening Takbīr, Qiyām when applicable, Qirāʾah, Rukūʿ, two Sujūd and the final sitting. Students should understand that Wajib errors and Fard omissions do not have identical legal consequences; the detailed correction rules are reserved for later study. Tranquillity, learning authentic recitations and respecting verified juristic differences are part of mature worship. Use a qualified teacher for a complete demonstration.

questions.q: Is Salah only a series of fast movements?
questions.a: No. It requires its prescribed actions and calm attention.

questions.q: What is Rukūʿ?

questions.q: What is Sujūd?
questions.a: Prostration during Salah.

questions.q: Are Fard, Wajib and Sunnah identical legal categories?
questions.a: No.

scenario: Your friend performs prayer movements very quickly to win a “speed record.” What could you say?
decide.feedback: Prayer is not a race. Encourage calm, correctly taught worship without shaming anyone.

lessons.title: Witr, Sunnah and Voluntary Prayer
story: On a quiet evening after ʿIshāʾ, Akhlaq saw his father preparing to pray again. “But the five daily prayers are finished,” he said. “Why are you praying more?”

Salaam explained the difference between the obligatory daily prayers and additional prayers taught in the Sunnah. He introduced Witr, which has a distinct Wajib classification in the Hanafi school. “Other Sunni schools describe its legal rank differently,” he added. “We follow a consistent taught method.”

Imaan asked how Witr was performed. Father explained the ordinary three-Rakʿah Hanafi method and the place of Duʿāʾ al-Qunūt, adding that they would practise the precise Arabic with a teacher rather than guessing the wording.

Akhlaq worried that if he did not know the full Qunūt by tomorrow, his learning had failed. Dadi Jaan told him to practise regularly and ask for instruction. “Learning a prayer takes effort,” she said. “It is not a race between siblings.”

The family also discussed Tahajjud, a voluntary night prayer. Mohsina wondered whether children should wake themselves until they were exhausted. Salamah answered that age, health and ordinary responsibilities matter.
Akhlaq added “steady learning” to the exhibition wall. He understood that extra worship should deepen gratitude and care—not become a competition in tiredness.

teaching.text: Witr follows the ʿIshāʾ prayer and is Wajib in the Hanafi school; the major Sunni schools do not all give it exactly that classification. The master chapter describes the three-Rakʿah Hanafi method and Qunūt. Sunnah and Nafl prayers provide opportunities for devotion, with legal distinctions among different prayers and their times. Children should learn authentic words with an approved teacher and build sustainable habits without treating optional worship as a public status display.

questions.q: How many Rakʿahs are taught in the ordinary Hanafi Witr method?

questions.q: What is Duʿāʾ al-Qunūt?
questions.a: A supplication taught in Witr in its prescribed place.

questions.q: Are all additional prayers legally identical?
questions.a: No. Sunnah and Nafl have differing usages and rulings.

lessons.title: Joining the Imam Without Racing
story: Akhlaq and Mohsin arrived at the masjid just as the congregational prayer began. Akhlaq wanted to sprint towards the front row before the Imam bowed. Mohsin caught his sleeve and asked whether rushing was appropriate.

After prayer, Sheikh Uncle explained the Prophetic instruction to approach prayer with calmness. A person who arrives late joins according to the proper method and completes what was missed. The detailed rules depend on the prayer and the person’s situation.

The children learned three words from the master chapter: Muqtadī, a follower; Masbūq, one who missed part of the congregational prayer; and Imām, the person leading. They practised listening for the Imam’s movements from a seated diagram rather than racing through a simulated prayer.

Imaan noticed that a younger child needed more space to move comfortably. She helped organise the class rows so the demonstration did not pressure anyone. Sheikh Uncle said that mosque manners include accessibility, quietness and respect.

Later Akhlaq wrote on the exhibition board: “Follow the Imam; do not compete with the Imam.” He had learned a practical lesson from arriving late: doing the right thing calmly is better than reaching the front in a panic.

teaching.text: Congregational Salah has recognised rulings about leadership, following and completing missed Rakʿahs. The master chapter distinguishes Muqtadī, Masbūq and Lāḥiq and gives more technical rules about different situations. At ages 9–10 we focus on arriving with calmness, joining correctly under instruction, following—not racing—the Imam and seeking help for missed-Rakʿah cases. Avoid inventing one universal rule for every late arrival, because school-specific details matter.

questions.q: Should a latecomer run to catch a Rakʿah?

journeys.title: The Blessings of Ramadan
journeys.aim: Fasting teaches restraint, gratitude and consideration for others.

lessons.title: Fasting: The Discipline of the Heart
story: During Ramadan, the academy organised a “Words Can Help” project. Imaan suggested the name after seeing an argument break out at lunchtime. Some pupils were fasting; others were not. One boy claimed that the children who were not fasting should not be allowed to help with the project.

Salamah reminded the class that fasting has rules about maturity, health and genuine excuses, and children must not be questioned publicly about personal circumstances. The purpose of the project was to practise kindness, not to inspect one another.

Akhlaq remembered that fasting is more than avoiding food and drink from the beginning of dawn until sunset. The Prophet ﷺ also taught the importance of guarding speech and behaviour. Akhlaq had been eager to argue; now he helped two classmates solve a disagreement peacefully.
Sir Zameer wrote “patience” and “self-restraint” on the board. Mohsin suggested a third word: “gratitude.” They discussed the blessings of water, time and the people who prepared food.

At home Akhlaq asked whether completing a fast made him better than his friends. Dadi Jaan said that worship should make us humbler and kinder, not proud. He helped set the table, offered a glass of water when appropriate and thanked the family for their care.

teaching.text: The fast of Ramadan is an obligation for those who meet its religious conditions, including maturity and ability. The master chapter teaches the dawn-to-sunset period and the moral aim of Taqwā. Children younger than religious maturity may be guided progressively where healthy and appropriate, but coercion, food deprivation or a public fasting leaderboard have no place in this curriculum. We should discuss kindness, duʿāʾ, truthful speech, patience and gratitude alongside the basic rules. Detailed invalidators and expiations belong at the advanced level.

questions.q: When is the daily fast of Ramadan observed?
questions.a: From the start of true dawn until sunset, under the prescribed rules.

questions.q: What does fasting teach beyond hunger?
questions.a: Self-restraint, patience, gratitude and guarding speech.

questions.q: Is every child obligated to fast in the same way as an adult?
questions.a: No. Religious maturity and other conditions matter.

questions.q: May we pressure classmates to reveal their fasting status?
questions.a: No.

reflect: Have I made life easier for someone during Ramadan?

scenario: A pupil misses a fast for a private reason. Should you question them in front of the class?
decide.feedback: No. Respect privacy and let families and qualified scholars handle individual rulings.

lessons.title: Taraweeh and Building Sustainable Habits
story: On the first weekend of Ramadan, Akhlaq wanted to stand for every possible extra prayer, recite the longest passages and still wake early for his school project. By the next morning he was tired and short-tempered.

Imaan helped him make a better plan. “We should learn the prayers correctly and also respect our health and duties,” she said. Their father explained the special standing in Ramadan and the practice of Taraweeh, while noting that its full Hanafi detail and recognised differences would be taught with a qualified teacher.

At the masjid, Akhlaq saw worshippers of different ages. An elderly person prayed seated, and a family with a young child left early. He was tempted to compare them, but Dadi Jaan reminded him that he did not know their circumstances.

The next evening he chose a sensible routine: revise one short Sūrah, attend worship with family when suitable, help clean up after Iftār and prepare for school. Mohsina added a daily Qur’an listening moment to the exhibition’s Ramadan wall.

The teacher praised their approach. Consistency, respect and correct worship mattered more than collecting public points for the longest time spent awake. Akhlaq finally felt that Ramadan could be a month of worship and gentleness together.

teaching.text: Taraweeh is the special Ramadan night prayer. The master chapter presents its traditional Hanafi method, congregational practice and relationship with Qur’anic recitation. Students should understand the purpose of Ramadan worship while learning specific method and Rakʿah details from a recognised teacher. A sustainable age-appropriate routine includes learning recitation correctly, keeping ordinary responsibilities and showing good conduct. Optional worship must not be turned into a contest or a reason to neglect health.

questions.q: When is Taraweeh associated with special worship?
questions.a: During the nights of Ramadan.

questions.q: Why does Qur’anic recitation have a special place in Ramadan?
questions.a: Ramadan is linked to the revelation of the Qur’an.

questions.q: Should extra worship make children disregard sleep and health?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Is worship measured by a classroom leaderboard?
questions.a: No.

reflect: Which small Ramadan habit can I continue after the month ends?

scenario: A friend claims anyone who leaves Taraweeh early lacks faith. Is that a fair judgment?
decide.feedback: No. We do not know another person’s circumstances or heart, and should encourage worship without shaming.

lessons.objective: Recognise Taraweeh as Ramadan night worship and form sustainable Qur’an and good-manners habits.
lessons.dailyAction: Choose one sustainable Ramadan habit for a week, such as a short Qur’an reading with family.
lessons.tryTogether: Design a gentle weekly routine that includes Qur’an, Salah, rest, helpful chores and family time.

journeys.title: Community and Compassion
journeys.aim: Our worship should protect the dignity and rights of those around us.

lessons.title: Zakah, Fitr and Giving with Dignity
story: The school wanted to collect supplies for families affected by heavy rain. Akhlaq proposed writing the donors’ names in enormous letters above the collection box. Mohsina asked what would happen to the children who could not contribute anything.

Salaam explained that giving should protect dignity. Zakah is not an ordinary prize for generous people; it is a prescribed duty on qualifying wealth and is directed to recognised recipients. Sadaqat al-Fitr has its own conditions connected to the end of Ramadan. Voluntary charity is another good form of giving.

“Can we calculate every family’s Zakah in our school exhibition?” Akhlaq asked. “No,” said Father. “Those calculations depend on many details of wealth, debts, time and legal responsibility. Qualified guidance belongs with the responsible adults.”

Imaan suggested a different project. Students could organise clean stationery, write kind notes and help sort supplies. Nobody would be forced to reveal how much their family had or whether they needed support.

At the end of the day Mohsin helped carry the boxes to a teacher. The class posted a sign that read: “Give with care. Receive with dignity.” Akhlaq liked it more than his donor leaderboard. It taught a better lesson about charity.

teaching.text: Zakah is a prescribed obligation with qualifying wealth, Niṣāb and specific recipients. The master text follows Hanafi rules and discusses Sadaqat al-Fitr and charity; some juristic details vary by school. Ages 9–10 can learn the differences among these forms of giving and the central idea that wealth brings responsibility. They should not calculate adult family liabilities, disclose finances or rank people by donation size. The rights and dignity of recipients are more important than publicity.

questions.q: What is Zakah?
questions.a: A prescribed obligation on qualifying wealth under its rules.

questions.q: What is Sadaqat al-Fitr connected to?
questions.a: The end of Ramadan, with its own conditions.

questions.q: Who is responsible for technical Zakah calculations?
questions.a: Appropriate adults with qualified guidance.

questions.q: How should people receiving help be treated?
questions.a: With dignity and respect.

reflect: When helping someone, do I think about their feelings and privacy?

scenario: A class wants to post which families donated the most. What would be a better approach?
decide.feedback: Protect privacy and focus on genuine assistance rather than ranking wealth.

journeys.title: The Holy Cities
journeys.aim: We study Hajj and Umrah in the correct sequence and connect worship to patient, helpful conduct.

lessons.title: Hajj: From Ihram to the Days at Mina
story: The final part of the school exhibition was a large map of Makkah and the Hajj areas. Imaan placed cards for Mina, ʿArafāt, Muzdalifah and the Sacred Mosque. Akhlaq tried moving the ʿArafāt card to the end because it made the map look more balanced.

Dadi Jaan explained that Hajj is not a sightseeing route. Its rites occur in appointed places and times. The master chapter follows the ordinary example of Tamattuʿ: a pilgrim completes Umrah earlier, leaves Ihram, then enters a new Ihram for Hajj. On the eighth of Dhul-Ḥijjah they go to Mina; on the ninth they stand at ʿArafāt; after sunset they travel to Muzdalifah; the tenth includes prescribed acts such as Rami, sacrifice where applicable, hair removal and Ṭawāf al-Ziyārah.

Akhlaq then asked about the eleventh and twelfth days. The family reviewed the three Jamarāt and the remaining rites, reminding him that detailed itineraries and conditions must be taught by qualified guides.

Mohsin noticed a problem on the map: it showed only arrows, no reminder to care for people. Imaan added a small panel about patience in crowds. The children left the map in its prescribed order. This was an act of worship, not a puzzle they could rearrange to earn points.

teaching.text: Hajj is the fifth pillar for Muslims meeting the religious conditions of ability. The source chapter teaches an illustrative Tamattuʿ route, distinguishing it from Ifrād and Qirān. Key stages include Ihram, Mina, standing at ʿArafāt, Muzdalifah, Rami, rites of the tenth day, Ṭawāf al-Ziyārah, Saʿī where applicable and the following days at Mina. Exact legal timing, permissions, exemptions and penalties are beyond a children's self-guided lesson. Our map is educational, not an operational itinerary or substitute for a trained pilgrimage guide.

questions.q: What is essential about the ninth of Dhul-Ḥijjah?
questions.a: Standing at ʿArafāt according to Hajj rules.

questions.q: Where do pilgrims go on the eighth in the example route?
questions.a: Mina.

questions.q: Does every pilgrim perform exactly the same type of Hajj?
questions.a: No. There are Tamattuʿ, Ifrād and Qirān with differences.

questions.q: May a learner rearrange Hajj rites to make a simpler map?
questions.a: No. They have prescribed order and timing.

reflect: How can patience protect people when a place is busy?

scenario: You want to push past an elderly pilgrim to reach an optional place faster. What is the right choice?
decide.feedback: Protect people from harm. An optional action is never a reason to push or injure others.

lessons.keyWords: Iḥrām — sacred pilgrim state; ʿArafāt — place of standing; Ramī — prescribed stoning; Ṭawāf — circumambulation.
lessons.parentNote: Keep the map general. No staged pilgrim crowds or sacred rites as physical games; check all dates, legal categories and real-world permissions.

lessons.title: Umrah: The Sacred Visit in the Correct Order
story: Akhlaq placed four cards on the table: Ihram, Tawaf, Saʿī and Halq or Qasr. He remembered some of their meanings from Volume 1 but wanted to understand their order. “Can we begin with cutting hair?” he asked.

Salaam explained that Umrah is a distinct act of worship with recognised rites. A pilgrim enters Ihram at the proper Miqāt, performs seven complete circuits of Tawaf around the Kaʿbah, performs seven traversals between Ṣafā and Marwah, and completes the visit by the required hair removal or shortening under the applicable rules.
Imaan counted the Saʿī crossings on a paper number line. “If I travel from Ṣafā to Marwah, is that one or two?” “One,” said Father. “The next crossing back is two.”

Mohsina wanted the exhibition to show children racing towards the Black Stone. Salamah said that touching it is not a condition of valid Tawaf and that harming worshippers is never justified for an optional act.

The children added an arrow labelled “care for others” alongside every step. Then they wrote a separate comparison: Hajj has appointed days and indispensable ʿArafāt standing; Umrah is a distinct sacred visit and does not replace Hajj. Their chart now taught order and good manners together.

teaching.text: The master Umrah chapter follows a Hanafi teaching framework: entering Ihram is a necessary condition; Tawaf is the central Fard act; Saʿī and the required hair removal are classed as Wajib. Other Sunni schools differ on some classifications. Children can understand the ordinary sequence and counting without attempting legal adjudication. Matters of menstruation, illness, missed acts, Miqāt travel, or penalties require private competent advice. Umrah is not merely visiting Makkah or praying in the Sacred Mosque.

questions.q: How many complete circuits are in Tawaf?
questions.a: Seven.

questions.q: How many traversals are in Saʿī?
questions.a: Seven, starting at Ṣafā.

questions.q: What completes Umrah after its other rites?
questions.a: The required Halq or Qasr according to the rules.

questions.q: Is Umrah identical to Hajj?
questions.a: No. Hajj has its own appointed rites, conditions and time.

reflect: Could I obey Allah and treat others patiently at the same time?

scenario: You cannot reach the Black Stone without pushing. Is pushing justified?
decide.feedback: No. Touching it is not required for valid Tawaf, and hurting others is wrong.

lessons.title: Returning Home: The Real Lesson of Pilgrimage
story: The exhibition was almost complete. Each group had prepared a table, but the final display felt too full of definitions. Akhlaq noticed that the visitors could explain where pilgrims travel without mentioning how they should treat one another.

Sheikh Uncle asked a question: “If someone returns from Hajj but continues to lie, push others and speak harshly, what important lesson have they missed?” Imaan answered that the Qur’an connects pilgrimage with avoiding wrongdoing and quarrelling. Sacred travel should encourage a person to improve everyday conduct.

The class designed a “Return Home” notebook. It had four prompts: Did I wait my turn? Did I speak gently? Did I respect someone with a disability? Did I correct a mistake? No one had to disclose personal religious acts. The notebook was a private reminder, not a competition.

Mohsin suggested a final exhibition activity: invite visitors to choose one small useful action for the coming week. A grandmother chose to call a relative. A pupil chose to stop interrupting. Akhlaq chose to apologise for mocking a classmate’s slow work.

On the final afternoon Sir Zameer looked at the completed exhibition. “You have learned many rules,” he said. “Now keep studying them carefully. And remember that the purpose of learning is to obey Allah and benefit people.”
Akhlaq closed his notebook with the words: “Guidance is a journey I keep living.”

teaching.text: Hajj and Umrah are prescribed acts of worship, not general character-building holidays. Yet their Qur’anic teachings include patience, avoidance of indecency and quarrelling, sincerity, care for others and responsibility. The final chapter in this student volume connects these lessons to life at school and at home without claiming that every good deed replaces a ritual obligation. It also concludes the ages 9–10 learning pathway: learners should be more accurate, compassionate, curious and ready for the advanced work at ages 11–12.

questions.q: What should pilgrimage teach about other people?
questions.a: Patience, dignity and avoidance of harm.

questions.q: Does knowing ritual names mean learning is complete?
questions.a: No. Correct practice and moral improvement matter too.

questions.q: Can a charitable deed replace prescribed Hajj for someone obligated to perform it?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: What is one thing a learner can improve after this volume?
questions.a: A specific act of worship, truthfulness, kindness or careful learning.

reflect: Which lesson in this book has most changed the way I treat someone?

scenario: A pupil says they will never need to learn anything more about worship after finishing this book. What would you say?
decide.feedback: Learning continues. We should practise what we know and seek further qualified guidance as we grow.
